title: Integrated employment support
summary: Integrated employment pathways across SNAP, TANF, and Medicaid that support compliance and long-term economic mobility.
body_markdown:
**Key takeaways**


Advancing economic mobility requires moving beyond job-placement metrics to support employment as an ongoing pathway, addressing real-world barriers, and helping individuals sustain and progress in work over time. By integrating technology, human support, and program alignment across SNAP, TANF, and Medicaid, states can design employment strategies that meet compliance requirements while enabling more durable, human‑centered outcomes.


## Connecting people to opportunity while reducing barriers to participation


*This article was featured in Policy & Practice magazine.*


Across public benefit programs, employment has long served as a cornerstone of efforts to support self‑sufficiency. Traditionally, success has been measured through participation milestones or job placements, indicators that allow states and participants to demonstrate compliance with[work‑related requirements](https://maximus.com/program-services/human-services/state-and-local-employment-and-training) .


Today, state and local human services leaders are increasingly asking whether these measures alone reflect what program participants need to remain employed and move forward over time. When job seekers face caregiving responsibilities, transportation gaps, health considerations, and changing work schedules, employment is an ongoing process. Supporting economic mobility begins with helping people connect to work, but it continues through sustained employment, adaptation, and progress toward greater stability.


For program leaders, the challenge is not whether employment expectations matter, but how to design systems that meet statutory requirements while supporting durable outcomes — at scale, within constrained resources, and in ways that reflect real‑world circumstances. Advancing economic mobility requires a shift from viewing employment as a transaction to supporting it as a pathway over time.


### A converging policy landscape across programs


This shift is relevant across[SNAP](https://maximus.com/state-and-local-government/snap) and TANF programs with long‑standing work requirements, as well as near-term[Medicaid](https://maximus.com/state-and-local-government/medicaid) community engagement requirements, where implementation models must come together quickly. Although these programs operate under different rules and funding structures, they increasingly share common objectives.


SNAP and TANF bring decades of operational experience engaging individuals around employment, training, and self‑sufficiency. Through real‑world implementation at scale, states and counties have refined approaches to outreach,[case management](https://maximus.com/program-services/case-management) , barrier resolution, and employer engagement.


Medicaid community engagement requirements introduce similar themes, though often with different approaches to compliance and member engagement. Across all three programs, agencies are balancing the need to meet statutory requirements with broader goals such as reducing churn, supporting ongoing participation, and promoting longer‑term stability.


The convergence of these policy goals presents an opportunity for states to adopt employment strategies rightsized to their specific contexts while drawing on proven approaches from across programs. Viewing employment as a pathway, rather than a one‑time transaction, can help align compliance, engagement, and mobility objectives.


### Moving from job boards to opportunity boards


Traditional job boards play an important role in connecting individuals to open positions, but most assume participants are equally ready to search, apply, and begin work. In reality, individuals approach employment from very different starting points.


An effective employment “front door” acknowledges this variability. Rather than offering a single search experience, opportunity boards organize options into guided pathways aligned to common goals and constraints — such as immediate income, short‑term training, schedule stabilization, or re‑entry after an employment gap. This framing helps individuals understand what is feasible now and how choices connect over time.


Choice works best when it is informed — when people can quickly see which options are realistic given their constraints and understand what comes next.


A skills‑first approach is central to this model. Opportunity boards translate lived experience — whether caregiving, military service, informal work, or prior employment — into usable skills and link them to attainable next steps. When additional preparation adds value, short‑cycle training and micro‑credentials can be presented alongside jobs, clarifying time commitment, credentials earned, and roles unlocked.


Opportunity‑based approaches also recognize that progress is not limited to immediate placement. Structured volunteer and community service roles can function as experience bridges, helping individuals build recent work history, references, and routines. Barrier‑aware filtering further ensures that choice is realistic — allowing individuals to focus on opportunities they can start and sustain based on schedule, transportation, physical demands, accessibility, and language.


When individuals are ready to move forward, the front door should connect to clear next steps, rather than becoming a dead end. Warm handoffs to partners, supported by confirmation and light‑touch reminders, help sustain momentum without forcing participants to navigate multiple systems on their own. At scale, trust and curation matter: opportunities verified and refreshed by local partners signal relevance, while feedback loops help states refine pathways based on what leads to sustained engagement and completion, particularly when paired with human support.


### Designing for real‑world barriers to employment


Individuals striving to meet work requirements often face intersecting barriers that shape whether an opportunity is viable over time. Transportation gaps, caregiving responsibilities, health considerations, digital access, and schedule variability do not affect individuals uniformly, and they can change quickly.


Effective employment strategies account for this variability rather than assume linear readiness. Some individuals benefit from streamlined access to job listings aligned to their constraints. Others require brief, targeted assistance or short‑term preparation before employment is realistic. In some cases, more comprehensive support is necessary to prevent repeated disruption.


Opportunity boards that surface practical context, such as proximity to transportation or childcare, help individuals quickly identify viable options without additional intervention. States can take this further through barrier‑aware filtering that reflects real constraints, including schedule stability, physical demands, language needs, remote or hybrid settings, and basic digital access. In some cases, short‑cycle training or credentialing is the more effective next step. Leading programs also link opportunity exploration to complementary supports that stabilize participation and improve retention over time.


Understanding employment through a whole‑life lens allows agencies to intervene thoughtfully, adding complexity only where it improves outcomes. A common framing among effective programs is “job today, job tomorrow.” Immediate employment can support income and compliance, while continued engagement helps individuals adapt to change, pursue advancement, and remain connected long enough for progress to take hold.


### Technology and human support working together


The strongest employment systems are defined not by technology or case management alone, but by how intentionally the two work together.


[Digital tools](https://maximus.com/customer-experience/digital-government) expand access and flexibility by enabling individuals to engage with volunteer, training, and employment options that fit their schedules and circumstances. Online platforms, text messaging, and phone‑based engagement can reduce barriers — particularly for rural or geographically dispersed populations — when paired with clear, plain‑language communication that makes requirements and next steps easier to understand.


When well designed, technology also supports warm handoffs to training providers or community partners and enables light‑touch reminders that help participants follow through.


At the same time, technology cannot account for every disruption. A missed shift due to a childcare closure or transportation change does not necessarily signal disengagement. Still, without timely support, these moments can quickly escalate into job loss or compliance challenges.


This is where human support adds the greatest value. Skilled caseworkers and coaches help interpret options, troubleshoot challenges, and provide problem‑solving support when it matters most. Their role is not to replace self‑service tools, but to complement them, intervening selectively to sustain momentum. Systems that reduce routine administrative work and surface relevant information allow staff to focus on higher‑value engagement when it matters most, strengthening both operational efficiency and participant experience.


### Aligning employment strategies to state context


For states administering SNAP, TANF, and Medicaid, employment strategies often span programs with distinct policy and funding constraints. While these differences complicate coordination, incremental alignment (where allowed) can reduce duplication, improve efficiency, and enhance the participant experience.


As states assess their approach, leaders must determine the level of support needed to meet current requirements. In many cases, opportunity platforms curated to local labor markets can efficiently connect individuals to qualifying activities and next steps, supporting compliance while minimizing administrative complexity.


Some states may choose to build on this foundation to pursue broader goals such as reducing churn, improving retention, or supporting advancement. In these models, shared employment infrastructure can support multiple programs while targeted human support and partner coordination address specific needs. Active deadline management — tracking response windows, issuing reminders, and escalating outreach when needed — helps ensure noncompliance is not the default outcome.


Regardless of model, successful strategies are grounded in the local context. Engaging workforce partners, employers, community‑based organizations, and training providers helps ensure employment supports reflect lived experience and real labor market conditions. Flexibility remains essential, allowing states to adapt as policy requirements and economic conditions change.


### Advancing mobility one pathway at a time


Economic mobility is built through systems, not single tools. As engagement expectations continue to evolve across SNAP, TANF, and Medicaid, state and local leaders have an opportunity to design approaches that meet today’s requirements while supporting longer‑term stability.


By treating employment as a pathway, rather than a transaction, agencies can align compliance, engagement, and outcomes in ways that are both operationally feasible and human‑centered. When employment supports are designed to reflect how people actually move toward work and stability, progress becomes achievable one pathway at a time, for individuals, families, and communities alike.


This insight also appeared in APHSA’s Policy & Practice Magazine.
